title: DNA Study Tracks English Language's Ancient Origins
paragraphs: A major new study using ancient DNA has shed new light on the origins of the Germanic languages, the family that includes English, German, Dutch and the Scandinavian languages.

The research, carried out by an international team led by Leiden University in the Netherlands and the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, was published in November as two articles in the scientific journal Nature. The team analyzed DNA from 712 ancient people and combined it with more than 4,000 previously published genetic profiles from across Europe and Asia.

For many years, researchers had believed that the Germanic languages descended directly from the language of the first migrants from the steppe, the grasslands of present-day Ukraine and southern Russia. These people reached Scandinavia about 5,000 years ago.

However, the new study suggests a rather different and more complicated story. It points to a second group of people who arrived in Sweden about 800 years after the steppe migrants, probably from the area of the present-day Baltic States. Within a few centuries, this group had spread across Scandinavia. Around 1,700 years ago, their descendants reached Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, Great Britain and northern Italy. The researchers believe that this second wave of migrants may have brought the language that later became Germanic.

The study also revealed a surprising and unexpected story about the Vikings. Around 1,500 years ago, a large-scale migration brought people from northern Germany to Denmark and southern Sweden, where they largely replaced the local population. This coincides with the emergence of Old Norse, the language of the Vikings. As a result, many Danish and Swedish Vikings shared common roots with the Anglo-Saxons who settled in England.
Guus Kroonen, a linguist at Leiden University, said that no one had seen this coming, adding that the findings rewrite the history of language.

However, the researchers emphasized that DNA alone cannot reveal which language people spoke. Their conclusions are based on combining genetic data with linguistic and archaeological evidence, and the link between the second migration and the Germanic languages remains a hypothesis.
